speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ARTS, LETTERS AND SCIENCES TABLING OP REPORT OF ROYAL COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to lay on the table copies, in English and in French, of the report of the royal commission on national development in the arts, letters and sciences.
The report was presented by the chairman of the royal commission at twelve o'clock noon today, and placed before the governor in council immediately before the meeting of the house this afternoon. The government has, therefore, not yet had any opportunity to give consideration to the report, and, in fact, none of the members of the government has yet read it.
My colleagues and I have, however, confidence in the members of the commission, and we have no doubt whatever that the report will constitute a valuable guide to our future national development in the fields which it covers, and that the recommendations of the commission will be of the greatest assistance to the government in determining appropriate policies for such federal action as may be desirable in these fields.
In accordance with previous indications I have given to the house, I wished to lose no time in having the report made available to members of parliament and to the public, both because of the widespread interest in its subject matter and because the report itself will obviously call for careful study and discussion, not only by members of the government and of parliament but by the public at large.
In tabling the report I should like, on behalf of the government, to express deep appreciation of the untiring and devoted service given to this task by the chairman and members of the royal commission since it was established two years ago. I am sure that the work of the commission and their report will be a significant milestone in the development of our national heritage.

speechtext:
All hon. members would, I am sure, wish me to draw attention to the presence in the gallery of the distinguished secretary general of the United Nations, Mr. Trygve Lie. We all welcome the presence of one who for more than five years has dedicated himself steadfastly to the promotion of the high purposes and principles set forth in the charter of the United Nations.
Mr. Lie was elected to be the first secretary general of the United Nations in February, 1946, and recently his term of office was extended for a further three years beginning February 1, 1951. Since assuming this high office, he has won general admiration and respeot for his devotion to the work of the United Nations in all its phases.
I am not sure that it is wholly proper to refer to the national origin of such a noted

Inquiries of the Ministry internationalist, but I think that I should remark that Mr. Lie had a very distinguished career in the public life of Norway as a lawyer, statesman and diplomat before devoting his whole time to the service of the United Nations. Apart from holding many important portfolios in the Norwegian government-he was, for instance, foreign minister of the government in exile during the war-he was head of the Norwegian delegation at the San Francisco conference which resulted in the establishment of the United Nations. At this conference he served as chairman of the commission which drafted the provisions of the charter relating to the security council.
All hon. members, I am sure, would wish me to extend to Mr. Lie on their behalf the warmest possible welcome to the House of Commons of Canada.

speechtext:

The house in committee of supply, Mr. Dion in the chair.
1.	Departmental administration, $336,942.

Last evening just before
;he house adjourned I rose to make a few -emarks, and the chairman very kindly :alled it eleven o'clock. A few moments ago [ asked a question of the Minister of Agriculture, and he said that he would mswer it when we came to deal with his istimates. I shall now present the question
Supply-Agriculture
again, since it is based on an urgent request from a couple of farmers who came to my office today. I repeat the question, so that the minister when he is answering other questions will answer this one. What is the cost-of producing a pound of margarine for the market as compared with the cost of producing a pound of butter for the market?
Since we have started to deal with these estimates I notice that a great many western members have taken up the cause of the farmers of the west. In all discussions on farming and administration of the Department of Agriculture the western members stick together as though they had a common cause in the interest of the western farmers. It is difficult to tell whether they are Liberals, Conservatives, C.C.F. or Social Credit. If there is a farmer's problem before the house they are all inclined to stick together, and thby get their demands granted by the government by so doing. We had an example of that not so long ago when all the members from the west took up the cudgels for the farmers and they were granted a subsidy of some $65 million.
In the course of their remarks some of the western members were inclined to think that the eastern members are not so much interested as they should be in the cause of the western farmers. But I say that the eastern members have always been and still are interested in the western farmers, and a large majority of them are doing more for the western farmers than the western members are doing for the eastern farmers and their problems.
I do not take any objection to the members from the west, of all political parties, grouping together and making one demand. In fact I congratulate them on their having a co-operative spirit. We in the east sometimes take our politics a little too seriously, with the result that the agricultural problems of the east are not getting the attention from the department or from the government that the western farmers get.
The one important problem at the present time-the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton brought it to the attention of the minister- is that of marketing our surplus potatoes. For the first time in this house or anywhere else the amount that was allocated to assist the potato grower to market his surplus product has been mentioned. As the minister stated yesterday, that amount is some $300,000. It has been allocated to New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island. This will not be more than $150,000-probably it will not be over $100,000-for Prince Edward Island. It is only a small item when

Supply-Agriculture
you compare it with the $65 million that the wheat growers received. When you compare these two amounts you see the unfair attitude taken by the department and by the government toward the eastern farmers. We have had discussions of the price' that was to be paid to take care of the surplus potatoes in our province. I understood it was to have been 44 cents a bushel. This is at least 16 cents below the cost of production. However, as I said a moment ago, no evidence has been given of an order in council having been passed to pay the farmers for their surplus potatoes.
In the discussion that took place yesterday on this matter I find quite a difference between the views of the minister and those of the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton. They seem to disagree as to how this price should be paid and how much each government is to pay. There is a little difference in our province, because at the time that this question was uppermost in the minds of the farmers a provincial election was in progress and the farmers, rightly or wrongly, were led to believe that they would get 22 cents from the starch factory, 22 cents from the local government and 22 cents from the federal government, which would make 66 cents. I do not say that the Minister of Agriculture put out that proposition, but it was current during the election. It was good campaign material, judging from the results of the election that took place on April 26.
However, there is some misunderstanding with regard to the payment of 22 cents from the starch factory. If they are unable to take all the product that is being offered, will the government, either the federal government or the local -government, take the amount that the starch factories are not able to take? In other words, instead of dumping two or three million bushels of potatoes, will the government pay the same price of 44 cents in our province, and a little higher price by the barrel in New Brunswick? That is a matter which the farmers are considering at this time when they are planting their potatoes. It would be of great assistance to most of them to know just how they are to be treated with regard to the dumping of potatoes, which will have to be done in many instances.
It seems strange that a good food such as eastern potatoes should be dumped when other parts of the world are experiencing famine. We know that the government endeavoured to assist the farmers of western Canada by selling wheat to some of these distressed areas-wheat that was not fit for dour purposes. I think they should have -,-onsidered at the same time selling millions
[Mr. McLure.l
of bushels of extra choice potatoes, instead of having them dumped, when food is so scarce.
I shall not deal with any other matters, with the exception of the one pertaining to potatoes. However I would ask the minister when- he replies, to answer these questions:
1.	Was there or is there a proposal to pay the -potato growers of New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island $300,000? If so, when was this proposal passed, and how much was allocated to the Prince Edward Island growers?
2.	Will the farmers be paid- 44 cents a bushel for all potatoes dumped?
3.	Will farmers who were forced to sell at very low prices receive a sum of money which will place them in the same position as those receiving 44 cents a bushel?
4.	Is there to be a plan for the marketing of potatoes in 1951, and, if so, will the minister outline that plan?

Mr. Chairman, yesterday afternoon and evening several matters pertaining to agriculture were discussed. I am sure hon. members from the maritime provinces will forgive me if I do not refer to the potato problem, because I do not know very much about potatoes-other than possibly the difference between mashed and French-fried.
One other subject of interest to wheat farmers was the international wheat agreement. The discussion was introduced, I believe, by the hon. member for Lake Centre, when he suggested- that the government should ask for a- renegotiation of the contract. This sounded all right. I do not know whether it would be beneficial or not. I think all will agree that all members of the government are interested in seeing that we get as much as possible for our wheat.
We come now to the subject which has been discussed at some considerable length: I refer to the South Saskatchewan dam Along with other hon. -members, if at al possible I am i-n favour of getting started or the dam. The suggestion was made that the work might be held up until the time o: another election. I suppose that was throw! into the discussion more or less as a joke. Mr. Thatcher: What do you mean, a joke' Mr. Smith (Moose Mountain):	Because
there would be no good reason for holding i up until the time of another election. I would take ten years to build the dam and if that would elect the present government the hon. member will be sitting where he i for a considerable length of time-at leas until after another two elections.

The suggestion was made that we are united on the subject and that we would not play politics with it. With this I agree. I have no criticism of the government I support in respect of its playing politics. The only quarrel I have is that at times they are not political enough, and I have been urging some of the ministers to realize that on occasions they should be a little more political.
The suggestion was made that the South Saskatchewan dam was required because we need more electricity in that province. In the constituency I have the honour to represent is found the chief supply of electricity for the province. This supply is found in the Estevan-Bienfait area; it is made possible by cheap coal. I am not going to discuss the question whether a supply of water would give us cheaper electricity than coal. I do know, however, that at Bienfait, south and east of Estevan, the coal companies supply the power commission with coal to make their electricity at a price of less than a dollar a ton. I am informed that on that basis we can manufacture electricity from coal at just about the same price as it can be produced from natural gas. I am not sure of the cost of electricity at Estevan, but I understand it is produced at the plant for less than one cent a kilowatt.
In the Estevan area we have been interested in getting a smaller dam on Long creek. I understand this is being held up because of a report which is expected from the international joint commission. I shall not discuss the matter further. I have discussed it with the minister on many occasions, and I shall speak to him privately again. However, if the South Saskatchewan development, which might be considered more important, does not go ahead, I would be hopeful that money would be made available for the dam at Estevan on Long creek.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the item carry?

I cannot let it carry just yet. If one may judge from what has been said by hon. members who spoke yesterday and today, I believe it can be said that the farmers, and people generally in the east, are agreeable to the development of the dam on the South Saskatchewan river. If the result will be the production of more wheat and flour, if it will make the western provinces more prosperous, then I am sure all the people in Canada will be in favour of it. There is no doubt in my mind that through the years it will pay for itself.
Yesterday the Minister of Agriculture said that as far back as 1947 he was sold on the idea. The minister has had four long years 80709-2301
Supply-Agriculture
to sell the idea to the rest of the cabinet, but, according to what he said yesterday, up to now that has not been done. We know that the hon. gentleman is one minister who is thoroughly familiar with his department, and we know also that he is a clever politician. I do not like to see projects of this kind carried over from year to year. If it was a good thing for Canada in 1947, it should be good in 1951; it should not be left until 1953 or 1954, just before an election, before work is commenced. Why put off until tomorrow what you can do today, if it is necessary and if it will make our country more prosperous?
I think the irrigation scheme is a proper one; it has worked out successfully in other parts of southern Alberta, and at various other places in Canada. There is no doubt it will be successful in the South Saskatchewan area. My late colleague, Mr. John R. MacNicol, who sat in the house for a number of years, talked about this project for many sessions. It was not a matter of selling the idea to the government, because the government must have known about it for a long time. The late Mr. MacNicol was an engineer by profession. He knew the area, and had travelled by river from one end of it to the other. He was convinced that the dam could be built, and that when built it would stay there.
Some Liberal members referred to the production of power, but I am not in favour of the dominion government developing power. It is quite all right to build a dam for irrigation purposes, but the production of power should be left to the provincial government or to a corporation similar to the Ontario hydro. After all, the C.C.F. government have been bragging about the situation in Saskatchewan, and I think they are quite capable of taking care of the power situation.
There is one question I should like to ask the minister which he can answer later. A few weeks ago the price of butter jumped ten cents a pound. I should like to know why that sharp increase occurred, and also why the price of margarine immediately jumped ten or twelve cents a pound. These things should be controlled. I am not going into the question of price control, because the chairman would stop me, but I think this is information we should have from the minister.

Mr. Chairman, I have no intention of saying anything about western wheat, because that is about all we have heard for the last eleven years I have been here. I have no objection to the western wheat farmer getting all he thinks he should get or should have got out of his wheat, but I do not think the treasury should be bled to meet the

Supply-Agriculture
losses that have been sustained. If the marketing was not done properly, then we should go back to where the fault lies rather than try to take it out of the treasury. That is all I have to say about that.
The dairy industry of Canada is in about the worst condition it has been in for a long time, for several reasons. One reason is the entry of cheap oils to be used in the manufacture of a spread as a substitute for butter. The dairy industry cannot compete against them. If the government or the Minister of Agriculture is not any more interested in the dairy industry than to let that sort of thing happen, then we cannot expect very much.
The minister is just one man.

You cannot compete against cheap oils. If people want to buy margarine, that is all very well, but the dairy industry cannot compete against such a spread. I suggest to the government that milk production should be pooled. I do not know whether any thought has been given to this in past years, but it should be considered. There is no reason why a farmer producing milk on one side of the road should receive a different price from that received by the farmer on the other side of the road simply because he sells to a creamery, a cheese factory, a concentrated milk plant or what have you.
Milk production should be pooled and the products sold at the same price according to grade. If it was handled in that way it could then be put into the production of whatever commodity was most needed. That is the only way you will ever have sufficient butter to supply the demand. You will not get it even at 58 or 60 cents a pound, because too many farmers are allowing calves to suck cows because they cannot see their way clear to working ten or fifteen hours a day and paying income tax at the same rate as other people who work only an eight hour day. A farmer must work ten or fifteen hours a day to get up into the taxable income bracket, while other people can make the same money working an eight hour day. If a farmer gets into the income tax paying bracket it is because he works long hours. There should be some adjustment.
I should like the minister to tell us why the price of hogs went down about four or five cents a pound a few weeks ago and yet the retail price of pork did not drop at all. Then the price rose again after a short period. The only one who suffered was the farmer.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to ask the minister where the Nova Scotia potato grower stands with regard to the subsidy on potatoes. There are quite a

few potato growers in Nova Scotia. It is true that they do not always have to take as low a price as the potato growers in Prince Edward Island or New Brunswick, but sometimes they have to take less than the 44 or 45 cents per bushel which was mentioned last evening and this afternoon.
I support the hon. member for Queens and the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton, who have asked for a support price for potatoes in the maritime provinces. This is a large item of production in those three provinces, especially in Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick. I do not see why a farmer who has put in long hours growing potatoes should have to sell them at 25 cents or 30 cents per bushel with no floor under his price, while the western farmer gets a good price for his wheat and has the benefit of a floor under his price. The same goes for butter. The potato grower should receive the same consideration. I want the minister to tell us why Nova Scotia was not brought under this agreement. It may be the fault of the provincial government. 1 understand they have a good marketing board in that province. I should like to see a support price for potatoes, to govern not only the old crop but to be carried forward in connection with the new crop.

Mr. Chairman, so that there may be no misunderstanding in the minds of the minister and hon. members I should like to put in a word for the newest province. There may be some who wonder whether we produce anything down there except fish. But we do grow some potatoes and other vegetables, and I submit that our dairy industry also should receive some consideration. We have a peculiar situation in that the United States bases fly in their milk from Prince Edward Island and thus by-pass the richest part of the newest province. It seems to me that the western part of the province could supply the needs of these bases.
When the minister replies, as I believe he will, I should like him to give us his views on price support. I believe he is entirely in favour of support and floor prices for agricultural products. I am satisfied that he has always felt that that is a good thing. I should like to know whether there is anything bad about floor prices. Is there any reason why floor prices cannot be applied to all commodities produced in Canada? Is there any disadvantage in putting floor prices under the different commodities produced all across Canada?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall the item carry?
I think the minister is willing to answer these questions before the item carries.

This is scarcely the time for cross-questioning. I think the best time for that is when we get to the items concerned.
I am quite prepared to give a general reply to what has been discussed, but I doubt very much if at this stage I should discuss every individual item. They are all covered under specific items. When we come to dairying we can discuss dairying much better than we can discuss it now.
On the general question which has just been referred to, I would say to the hon, member that I am going to Newfoundland on Sunday.
You are very welcome.

I intend to spend three or four days there next week and make myself better acquainted with their situation in relation to agricultural production. I hope that following that visit I shall be in a better position to discuss matters of that kind. I would point out, however, that the only criticism I heard from Newfoundland with regard to potatoes came at the time of our conference last year, when it was being suggested that we should subsidize the marketing of potatoes in Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick.
What about Nova Scotia?

Nova Scotia of course had put forward their suggestions too. However,
I was told that the practice in Newfoundland had been to encourage their people to produce potatoes for consumption by those who live in Newfoundland, and that the practice of the government in the past had been to encourage a rather higher price for potatoes. They had developed a condition under which the farmers were able to prodhce their potatoes and obtain for them, in the local markets, prices which paid them fairly well. They took some objection to our subsidizing the marketing of potatoes to make it possible for someone to come in and undersell them. I think there is some reason in that. It was definitely stated at the time that they did not follow along with some others who were advocating another policy.
On the general question of the marketing of potatoes, we have no objection whatsoever to doing the same thing in one province as in another. It is for that reason that we have insisted on the producers in Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick organizing under some system that could be applied in other provinces if other provinces wished to apply it. The system now being followed there in connection with the marketing of surplus potatoes for this past year is that of making
Supply-Agriculture
use of the Agricultural Products Co-operative Marketing Act under which they set up boards which take delivery of the potatoes and pay to the producer a certain initial payment.
The suggestion was made a few moments ago that 22 cents a bushel is paid by the people who process the potatoes into starch, and I think that is about the correct figure. It was also suggested that someone else was going to pay some other amount. Everything that has to do with that is written into the agreement, and, so far as I can recall, the only order in council-I do not have it here at the moment, but it will be here later when we come to that matter-is the one giving me authority to sign the agreement. The agreement is with the marketing boards in Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick. If Nova Scotia desires a similar agreement, it will be necessary first for the producers in Nova Scotia to form a similar organization and come here with the idea of obtaining similar support.
Dairy products were referred to, and I notice that the member who asked some of the questions is not here at the moment; but there was a general question having to do with the price of butter at different times.
I might tell him, and others who are interested, something that apparently is not generally understood. There never was a time last year when we were short of butter in Canada. As a matter of fact we had 10 million pounds of butter still in storage on the first of April, which is a higher amount than we had in seven out of the last eleven years. The first of April is the beginning of the month when our production again reaches the amount of our consumption. There was no shortage of butter in Canada at any time last year. I think if we start from there we can reason much more-
Why did you import some?
We did not import any. As a matter of fact we tried to stop some people from importing it, but they did import it.
The government allowed the importation of the butter.

Eventually, after it was
purchased, and purchased in spite of our views on the matter, we permitted that butter to come in, with the suggestion that it was to be put absolutely at our disposal when it came in; but that was not done. All that can be fully explained when we come to discuss dairy products.
I should like to ask the minister a question.

My hon. friend asked me to make a speech on this matter, at the

Supply-Agriculture
outset, and if he will permit me to make it, we -can have a discussion when we come to dairy products.

The question is relevant.
The minister has referred to butter, and I think this would be the right time to ask the question.
Ask it.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The hon. member will realize that on the first item we have a general discussion. The Minister of Agriculture is now giving a general reply to the general discussion which has taken place. However, when it comes to answering questions, I think the practice has been to wait until the specific item is before the committee.
Mr. Chairman, in any debate in this house a member may rise and ask a speaker if a question can be asked. Why is there any objection? The minister is willing to answer.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra will understand that whenever an hon. member wants to ask a question of the member who has the floor, that member must give his consent.
The minister has.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Usually the member who has the floor acknowledges that he consents to reply to the question by taking his seat. The Minister of Agriculture took his seat, as did the hon. member for Brant-Wentworth, when I stood up. Therefore it was apparent that he was not giving his consent. As a matter of fact he said that he would deal with it when we come to the item. That is by no means giving consent to the question asked by the hon. member for Brant-Wentworth.

Mr. Chairman, the minister said he would allow the question, so I think it would be all right. Why did the government not give out information regarding the number of pounds of butter being held by the government if there was no scarcity?

The government not only gave out the information, but I read it very carefully from my place in the house. If the hon. member will refer to Hansard for this session he will find that at the time I announced the floor price for butter for the coming year as 58 cents, I pointed out clearly, and emphasized the fact that there had not been any shortage of butter, and there was not any shortage on the first of April of this year. We had approximately 10 million pounds.
That was long after the price had gone up to 85 cents.
It was not long after the price had gone up to 85 cents. It was just about in the middle of the experience.

Who got the difference
between the price at which it was brought in and the price at which it was sold?

If we had followed the policy my hon. friend has been advocating for some years, they would have had that margin all the time. As a matter of fact by following the policy we did, butter was absolutely controlled during all the time that we had butter. We had butter until the week of March 24. While we had butter the price remained at 62 to 64 cents, but when the government had no more butter-butter was still in the country, nevertheless, in storage- the price went up as high as 84 cents. I believe a question which is just as important as why it went up is why it went down again. It went down 12 cents in two days. I have a better idea as to why that happened than I have as to why it went up. I can explain that fully when we come to discuss dairy products. It is for that reason we are interested in seeing to it that the government does have some control over the product, and for the last two years we have been attempting to have that control.
At the end of the year preceding the one about which we are now talking, we were accused of having too much butter, and we had 28 million pounds. Everyone said that was too much, and we should not have had it. It was a surplus that we could not sell. Then, when we got down to' 10 million pounds we were told we did not have any butter at all. Going back over the years we have found that when we had 10 million pounds on the first of April we had all the butter we ought to have. In the years preceding this year, the men who are now being accused of having taken too much for butter always had the right to charge more for butter in the wintertime than they paid for it in the summer. When a committee of this house investigated the matter a few years ago, it was admitted by those who are now being accused of having taken too much for butter and margarine that they did have a margin of profit of about 12 cents a pound on butter. I have not any doubt that for the short period of two or three weeks this spring these people had a margin which gave them a considerable profit.
The question which has been asked is, why did this government not do something about it? The real answer to that is that the authority is with the province. During that period any one province in which butter was stored could have controlled the butter. This government has no control over prices in

that sense except during wartime. The trouble with some of my friends is that all their experience in public life has been during wartime or since the war, and they believe the authority of this government is the same in peace as it is during a war.
How could the provinces control the price?

In exactly the same way as they now control the price of milk. A further suggestion is made that we should do something to ensure that the price of milk for all purposes is the same. Again that comes under the control of the provinces. There is an organization already set up under the provincial legislation to handle cheese in Ontario. There is no reason in the world why they cannot handle all the milk, butter, and everything else that is produced from milk in the province of Ontario in the same way as they are handling cheese under that act. Each time the question has been discussed here the method suggested is the same method as being used in connection with potatoes in the maritimes, namely that the milk be delivered to one central farmers' co-operative, and that the same price be paid for the milk no matter what use is going to be made of it. Then, there should be a final payment made on the same basis. That has been operating with regard to whole milk in every province in Canada ever since milk boards were set up, but it has not been operating in connection with milk which goes into the production of cheese, butter and canned milk.
In so far as whole milk is concerned there were quotas set before the war ever started, and the price was set. An individual was told the price at which he could sell whole milk, how much of it would go to the cheese factory or somewhere else, and that was just the beginning of the plan suggested by the hon. member. I am sure that every dairy farmer in Ontario realizes that is a matter which could be handled under the present provincial legislation in the province of Ontario, and it has been handled that way for some considerable time.

I did not intend to make any remarks at this time, but I cannot let the minister get away with the statements he has just made regarding butter. It is not good for the industry to have butter prices as high as they were this winter. The minister says that we were never short of butter. On the one hand, he tells us that the price did not go up until after the government stores were depleted, while on the other he tells us the government had 10 million pounds.

I did not say the government had 10 million pounds. I said that there

were 10 million pounds in storage, but we did not have it. The trade had it, and they charged what they liked for it.

Is it not a fact that the government did allow a further importation of 4-5 million pounds of butter, knowing very well that there were still 10 million pounds in the country, and also allowed the trade to make practically half a million dollars' profit on that transaction?
That is not true either, but go on and make your speech.

According to a statement the minister made at Macdonald college the price of that butter to the trade was 40-4 cents. I have not the clipping containing that statement here, but I have it in my office. That is the minister's own statement.

The price of that butter to the men who purchased it, laid down in Halifax, was 56-5 cents. Never at any time have I said it was 40 cents. I have said that if it had been delivered in Canada at the same price at which it was sold to the British, it could have been delivered here at 40 cents, but it was not.
Obviously, then the minister was misquoted because the 40 4 cents was mentioned in the clipping.

Well, I have not seen that.
I have seen the statements in most newspapers, and they have never said that. The statement I made on the subject appeared in Hansard, and you can read it there and check if.
I can bring the clipping down and read if to the minister. I used it in the budget debate, but the minister was not here so it was lost.
Then it is not a correct statement of anything I have ever said. What I have said is in Hansard, and the hon. member can read if there.

It is rather odd, Mr. Chairman, that that is the only time the 40-4 cent price ever appeared in a newspaper or anywhere else. Every other time this 56*5 cent price has been given out. I wonder whether the trade was a little displeased about that price being quoted by the minister at Macdonald college. It appears obvious that they may have been. There is no doubt that it was in that clipping dealing with the speech the minister made at Macdonald, and it was not refuted when I quoted it in the budget debate.

In order to get the record straight, the first time that statement was

made was during a speech I read to the federation of agriculture in the city of Calgary. It is all on the record. I read it in the newspapers, and it was broadcast.
I heard it.
It does not come under my estimates. I do not think I can. It is under finance. The farm loan board is administered under the Department of Finance. It is not administered under my department.

My hon. friend heard it, and he knows what I am now stating is correct. The statement was that if butter had been laid down in Canada on the same basis as it was sold to the British it could have been laid down here at 40-4 cents.

There is no use arguing about it until I get the newspaper clipping; then I shall let the minister see it. It will prove to him that he did make that statement, or he will probably say he was misquoted.

There is one matter which I should like to bring to the minister's attention. Many young farmers in my riding have written to me concerning the difficulties they are experiencing today in buying land. This is due to the high cost of the land, and the amount of equipment that is required on a farm. Many of these young people are finding it extremely difficult to get into farming on their own. As a result of that many of these young people are drifting into the cities, and there is an increasing amount of land being worked by tenant farmers. I believe the Saskatchewan federation of agriculture presented a brief to the cabinet a short time ago making this recommendation, and I should like to put it on Hansard.
We recommend that the federal farm loan act be amended to make provision for a program whereby fully qualified young farm people under proper supervision may secure the greater part of their capital which would be repaid on a long term amortization basis.
I presume that other provinces have the same problem. I should like the minister to tell me today whether or not the federal farm loan act could be amended in some way so that it would enable these young farmers to purchase their land at least partially through a loan. Perhaps the province should contribute some part of it. Maybe there could be a dominion-provincial agreement. But I should like to tell the minister that this is a serious problem for many of our young rural people. I do not know what the answer is but I think it should be feasible that this federal farm loan act should be extended so that young farmers could buy their farms.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall the item carry?
No. I wonder if the minister can tell me if that matter is being considered?
Does the minister care to make a statement with regard to what I had to say about hogs a little while ago? I think the farmers of this country have been extremely kind to the packers.

Again this is one of those questions that we could deal with better when we come to hogs. But as I remember the statement, it was to the effect that some time a few weeks ago hogs went down three or four cents.
Yes.

Then I had said to someone here just while the hon. member was asking about that: I wonder if he wants me to tell him why they went up again three or four cents a few days later. Then he proceeded to ask me that question himself. I cannot keep track of all the changes in price that take place at Toronto, London, Stratford or wherever one might be delivering his hogs. I know that there was for a few days a drop in the price of hogs. Then in a few days hogs went back up again. In other words, I presume that the persons who were buying hogs had a scare of some kind of something that was done in the United States or something somebody said we were going to do here, and the bidding was down; or there may have been too many hogs on some markets, and the bidding was down for a few days. But whatever happened, the price of hogs went up again inside of a few days.
Again that is a matter which is not under our control. If an Ontario farmer delivers a hog to anybody in the province of Ontario, the price control with regard to the delivery of that hog is under the provincial authority and not the federal. If a farmer tries to deliver a hog over into Manitoba, that is another question. But if one farmer is delivering a hog in the province of Ontario to somebody there, the only control over that transaction is with the province.

I should just like to say one further word. The fact is that you have to deliver your hogs at a certain weight. If you keep hogs over a certain weight, you will be docked. When there is a heavy run of hogs or a delivery of hogs, down goes the price two or three cents, and those farmers who have those hogs lose that money. There is nothing fair about that. The buyers seem to know exactly when to put that price down a few cents; they get a nice run of hogs and then

back up again it goes. I do not think there is any other reason in the world for it than to get a few cheap hogs.

I am sorry to have to refer to this matter again, but the minister just said that the farm loan act would come under the Department of Finance. I realize that he is correct about that. But at the same time I know that there is no use of that coming up under finance unless the Department of Agriculture thinks that this scheme would be feasible; that is, of providing capital loans to young farmers who are trying to get started.
Why not to young loggers?

We help many people who live in the cities to buy their homes. Why would it not be just as sensible to have an act something like the National Housing Act so that young men in rural parts of the country could become established on farms? That is the only way that I can see that we are going to be able to prevent this continuous drift to the cities. I wish the minister would just say whether the department has considered that procedure. If it is not feasible -and maybe it is not-I wish he would tell us.

The present provision of the farm loan act, as I recall it, is that one must have security equal to about 50 per cent. Perhaps I am going too far when I say it is in the act. It is at least in the regulations under which the act is administered. One who is making a loan from the farm loan board must be able to give security equal to 50 per cent of the loan at least. That is where the young man runs into his difficulties. He says: I cannot give security equal to 50 per cent. It is not considered wise to make loans on any other basis at the rate at which the loans are made under the farm loan act. As I recall it, the rate is 4J per cent. It is considered that if you were going to take any greater risks than are taken, you would have to have a higher rate. That is the answer that always comes back when anyone applies for a loan on a farm. They say: How much security can you give? If the young man is able to give 50 per cent security, he can get the loan. If he is not, he may find some difficulty in getting it, unless he can get someone who is willing to give that 50 per cent security for him.

If I may, I just want to say to the minister that a few years ago that was not too bad when the amount involved was only $1,000 or several thousand dollars. But today, with the high cost of land and the high cost of equipment, even $10,000 in my 80709-231

I have the quotation from Hansard here. Obviously I must have read the clipping, in view of the fact that it appears in Hansard. I can get the clipping later and show it to the minister. But if I may be allowed to do so, I should like to read the quotation as it appears in Hansard, as taken from the Globe and Mail of March 1, 1951. It is as follows:
Food Producers Merit Fair Prices, Gardiner Holds
Ste. Anne de Bellevue, Quebec, Feb. 27-Canadian Press-Agriculture Minister Gardiner said today that Canadian food producers have two primary objectives-to produce enough food for our own people and to sell at a sufficiently high price to encourage them to keep on producing. New Zealand butter, which Mr. Gardiner said the government did not want to see brought into Canada, was laid down at Halifax at a cost of 40-4 cents a pound. The floor price in Canada was 53 cents. Canadian farmers could not compete with New Zealand butter. The butter dealers were selling the imported butter at 56J cents a pound.
"The market price in this country must be comparatively high," said the minister.

That is obviously pretty badly mixed up. I have here the statement which was made. It is as follows:
Britain would have been quite prepared to buy all New Zealand's surplus, but New Zealand thought she could sell considerable outside the agreement at a higher price. She asked to have 10 per cent released from the agreement, but after considerable negotiation Britain got 92 per cent-
Since this speech was made I learned that she really got 90 per cent.
-at 33-3 cents per pound f.o.b. New Zealand. This is equivalent to 40-4 cents landed at Halifax.
The New Zealand Co-op sold the 8 per cent to Canadian importers at 56J cents a pound landed at Halifax.
My hon. friend listened to this statement when it was read to him and others at Calgary. Why does he try to make me say something else, when he sat and listened to me read it? It does not matter what the Globe and Mail says I said. He knows what I said1.

If the minister is saying that I did not read the article right, may I say that I read only what is in the article. I did not hear what he said in Macdonald.
I only heard what he said at Calgary.

It is just the same as what I said everywhere. The statement continues:
The New Zealand Co-op sold the 8 per cent to Canadian importers at 56i cents a pound landed at Halifax. If you deduct 5 cents for duty, this leaves about 11 cents a pound profit over the British price.
That is the statement. Different arguments were based upon that statement but these are the facts in connection with it.

I have a few remarks to make before this item is carried. Before I start my remarks I wish to say that hon. members on this side of the house and over there in what we call the "rump" are very thankful for the effort the Minister of Agriculture is making to help agriculture all the way through. If the bom. member for Brant-Wemtworth would be a little more helpful to the Minister of Agriculture instead of jumping on him with both feet at every chance he gets we would get along a little better.
It has been clearly demonstrated this afternoon that those who want to obtain a federal subsidy on potatoes have to work through the provincial governments. The provincial governments have to ask for it. When.' I mentioned potatoes in Manitoba last year I was told that the amount produced there did not warrant a subsidy. However I want to assure the Minister of Agriculture that the hundreds of farmers along the Red river, both north and south of Winnipeg on both sides of the river, produce hundreds of thousands of bushels. If other governments are applying for a federal subsidy then I shall have to make it my business to inform the provincial government of Manitoba to apply for the subsidy on behalf of those farmers out there. They are not blaming the Minister of Agriculture for not paying a subsidy heretofore. The sole responsibility will be put on the provincial government.
A little while ago butter was mentioned. I am in agreement with some of the hon. members who have criticized the amount of labour it takes to produce a pound of butter and the amount of labour it takes to produce a pound of margarine. There is a great difference in producing a pound of margarine as compared with a pound of butter. It takes much more labour to produce a pound of butter. It is up to this government to stop the seal oil and whale oil coming in at low prices. It is coming in at 23 cents odd, and last year it was as low as 11 cents odd. Since I happen to have a little invested in the whale oil business myself I know what it is being purchased for. Last year Canada Packers purchased from the Adanac Whale and Fish Company many thousands of gallons of oil at 11 cents odd a gallon, and that same oil is being manufactured into margarine.
It was 11 cents a pound.

Eleven cents a pound, rather. Here is something to which I object rather strongly. The people of Canada are told by the press in big headlines that now you can colour Parkay margarine in two minutes or less. In other words, they are trying to make the white margarine into a package that looks like butter, and therefore they are trying to

fool the public. Hundreds of thousands of dollars are paid out in advertising margarine. If the public is going to fall for that stuff it is their fault. It would be to the advantage of the dairy farmers and the dairy producers all through the country to counteract these margarine advertisements in the paper and tell the people just what they are getting for their money.

We are now discussing agriculture. Until something comes along to displace it, I think we would be doing the farmers of Canada a great disservice if in the House of Commons we did not come to their protection. The farmers in the House of Commons are unorganized and do not stand in the same category as hardware men, lumber producers, or any of these high-powered selling organizations.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: And they never got $65 million.

I wish the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance would address the Chair when he speaks. That $65 million refers to agriculture, too. I would tell him, however, that it will be a long time before the farmers of Canada will have anything like 90 per cent of parity.

I should like to ask the minister two general questions. Perhaps they should be asked later, but this would seem

Supply-Agriculture
to be an opportune time. The first has to do with the over-all policy of the Department of Agriculture. Since we have been discussing wheat at this session, and since so many people from other parts of Canada seem to feel so unhappy because the farmers of the west are given some consideration, I wonder if it would not be wise for the minister to lay down the over-all policy of the government in respect of agriculture. Is not the government trying to be just as fair to the potato producers in the maritime provinces as it is to the wheat producers? Is there any such thing as discrimination between the treatment of one group and that of the other? I do not believe there is. But if the minister were to lay down what the policy is it would prevent those who represent certain other portions of agriculture from everlastingly making remarks to the effect that the amount they are getting is not fair.
We never got $65 million.

And we have to take all that kind of nonsense, too. Why do not the members from the maritimes get up and make a plea for their own welfare, rather than criticize others? Why do they not do something positive? Let them state what they want and why they want it, instead of everlastingly whining and complaining because others are getting what they are seeking.
The same thing applies to Ontario. As a member of parliament I am prepared to support the interests of agriculture in any part of the country-and I do not care what part it is. I expect all people from all parts of the country to feel the same way about it. The sooner we all do that, instead of acting like a lot of silly crabs, the better we shall get along. But we should have a policy laid down so that every member will realize that there has been an attempt to treat all parts of the country fairly.

Mr. Chairman, I suggest the
language being used by the hon. member for Lethbridge in respect of the maritime provinces is unparliamentary, and that he should withdraw it. He referred to maritime members as whiners and crabs. I suggest that, in a manly fashion, he should withdraw those remarks.

If my remarks have
offended the hon. member, then, in as manly a fashion as I can, I shall withdraw.
I should like to mention one further matter. I believe we are safe in saying that the business of agriculture is to see to it that we have the food for Canada that we need, and that we have food for export where we can export it profitably. Would the minister tell the committee what the general policy of the

government is toward ensuring adequately the production of various commodities in Canada we are going to need. I am sure the minister has some policy in mind, but it has not been stated before the house up to the moment. For instance, I have been alarmed, as I am sure other hon. members have been, to see the number of milch cows being so rapidly depleted in Ontario. To my mind that would seem to be a completely unsound situation, and I would like the minister to tell us in a general way what the Department of Agriculture has in mind to balance up the over-all production in Canada so that we shall not be running into the danger of a shortage of milk in various parts of the country.
I hope I have made my two requests clear. I am asking, first, for the over-all policy of the government in its attempt to be fair to the producers of all kinds of food in Canada, whether it be in connection with the production of potatoes, cheese, pork, beef, wheat or any other commodity. Secondly, I would like the minister to state the over-all policy pursued by the government in an endeavour to maintain a proper supply position in Canada, so that our granary, our pantry, our larder, whatever we choose to call it, will be normal and equal to the demands which may be made upon it.

Mr. Chairman, I do not know whether it would be as convincing for me to outline a plan or the plans which have been put into effect, and I do not know just why I should be asked to do it. At page 1494 of Hansard for this session, I placed on record at the request of hon. members the results of the policy.
I think it was agreed then that we had paid $731 million over a period of about ten years to the farmers in subsidies, premiums and payments of other kinds, including somewhere in the neighbourhood of $18 million a year in freight assistance in order to make it possible to have many of these products produced at a cost lower than they otherwise would have been produced for a considerable section of Canada. Anyone who examines that record will agree, I suggest, that we did divide the money as equally as possible among all the farmers, in accordance with their needs, at the time the action was taken.
That general policy has been carried out since 1944 under the Agricultural Prices Support Act, which I hold here in my hand. One member after another has risen in his place and suggested that we should follow the policy that has been followed in the United States. I do not like to make critical statements about what has happened in another country; but one has only to mention

3G27
what did happen in connection with potatoes, which have been discussed here today. One need only mention what happened in connection with eggs, and in connection with other farm products which are more or less perishable because of the policy of encouraging production which was followed in the United States.
You may follow policies which are based upon some formula that some college professor works out-and they may lead you farther than expected. These formulae which are supposed to settle everything are all very nice when they are set out, but when you see the results of some of them you hesitate to put them into effect. We have not followed the plan in that regard which has been followed in the United States. In other words, we have not set parity at a certain level and said that we were going to guarantee 90 per cent of parity. We said something a little different. In order to recall to hon. members' minds what we did say, I am going to read one section of the act of 1944 under which assistance has been given to farmers in whatever section of Canada they may be living and whatever they may be producing. Section 9 of the Agricultural Prices Support Act reads:
(1) For the purposes of this act, the board shall, subject to and in accordance with regulations made by the governor in council, have authority

I would suggest that farmers -and I am speaking of the general run of farmers, not some fellow who is farming on $500 an acre land just outside the city of Toronto or some other place-who are milking half a dozen to a dozen cows on their farms, and farmers in our section of Canada where all the surplus butter is produced if there is any produced, have produced it for very much less.

That is true.
The real cost is in between what?

Seventy-five and twenty-five. Fifty-eight cents is not very far from halfway between. In any case, after giving consideration to all the facts as they were presented to us we said: We will buy any butter that is offered to us at 58 cents. We said that one year and we got 60 million pounds. We said 53 cents the next year and we got 34 million pounds. We have said 58 cents this year and up until today we have not got any, but that does not mean we will not get any between now and next fall. We may get some at 58 cents some time. If we do not it will be because butter is selling at a higher price right across Canada, and for no other reason. Figured on the same basis as 58 cents was, I am told that butter is now selling at approximately 63 to 64 cents. If it is, the farmer is selling in a market that is 5 cents higher than the floor that we set, and I do not think any farmer is going to criticize the fact that he is getting 5 cents more.

I do not know just what our position is going to be next winter, but we have taken care of that as far as we can in making provision that this coming year if any butter is imported from New Zealand it will be imported by the government. That provision has already been made, and that fact has been made known to our friends in New Zealand. Therefore we think the matter is pretty well under control. Is the minister in a position to tell the country why wheat was not included in this act? What is there about wheat that puts it in a class by itself, so that it has to stand out in the storm?

The main answer to that is the statement which was made on the floor of the house at the time-1944-a part of which has been quoted quite a few times. When we put this act through to provide $200 million with which to take care of difficulties that might arise in connection with other farm products, it was clearly stated at that time that if it became necessary to handle wheat under the conditions that existed in the thirties, it could not be done with $200 million. It was suggested that wheat be left out of this act. Just to indicate the difficulty to the committee, I remind members that in the areas where wheat is grown we paid out $186 million for relief in the thirties. With all the experience that was behind us we thought, and I believe we were right, that if we brought a measure into this house saying that we were going to spend $200 million on all farm products including wheat, most representatives of farm constituencies in this country would have said that wheat would get all of it. Wheat was left out. It was definitely said at the time that if it were ever necessary to deal with wheat it could be dealt with under the wheat board which is definitely set up for the purpose of marketing wheat. I have just one more question following along the lines of the questions I have asked of the minister concerning wheat. By what criterion would the government determine the point at which it would become necessary to assist the v.'heat grower?

I must say that it is not really in our hands at all. It comes under the Department of Trade and Commerce, because that department is handling the marketing of wheat. Perhaps I should not say it does not come under our department at all, because the matter of production is under this department as well as the provincial departments. What we do say to the provincial governments when they -ask us to help

Supply-Agriculture
the wheat grower is that the province is responsible for providing seed, for example. This spring many of the farmers said that the seed was not good. The oats were frozen, the barley was frozen, and they were really concerned about sowing wheat that was frozen. Some of them wrote to us and asked whether we were going to assist with seed. We wrote back saying that that was a provincial responsibility.
When they come and ask us for assistance because the farmers are experiencing difficulties, we would say that our assistance is provided through the Prairie Farm Assistance Act. We contend that any assistance which should be given by the dominion government is made avalaible through that act. If there is to be any further assistance to individuals it ought to be made by the province or the province and municipality combined. That is the line of discussion which takes place.
In the matter of marketing wheat, it is marketed under the wheat board. The question has not really arisen since the passing of this act. The main belief when this act was passed was that, long before this, the bottom would have fallen out of farm prices. The bottom has not fallen out of farm prices. The problem that was really in people's minds when this act was passed has not arisen. We have made provisions for floor prices under the act in connection with farm products, and they have been set at a level which was never anticipated when the act was passed.

I am not sure that I conveyed to the minister just the question that was in my mind. If I recall correctly, he used words somewhat like these when he was discussing the act a moment ago; that if the time ever did come when it would become necessary to assist the wheat producers-do I quote substantially the minister's remarks?
That is what I said in 1944.

What I am trying to give the minister an opportunity of expressing to the house, as I am sure he is able to do, is this: By what criterion would he determine, at any given point, whether or not the time had come when it was "necessary" to assist the wheat growers?

I would only say that if it became the opinion of the government that wheat should be dealt with under this act it would be dealt with in just the same manner as are all other farm products. We made a complete record of the prices of farm commodities, or at least the board that was set up under this act made a complete record of the prices of farm products over a three-year period, 1944 being the third year.

At that time the farmers said: We have had the best return for our farm products, over 1942, 1943, and 1944, that we ever had in our history. They said: We want that position maintained as long as it can be maintained. We said: All right, we will try to do that under this act. We therefore made a record of the prices and, so far as we could, of the costs of production at that time.
That record is there. When we come to consider what ought to be done this year with regard to any product, we go back and check with that record. When we last discussed this question the hon. member for Brant-Wentworth was present, as were one or two other members of the house, down at Niagara Falls two years ago, I think it was, at the federation meeting. We had the United States authorities there. Both the United States authorities and Mr. Hope, who checks these matters for the farm federation, finally stated at that meeting that our bases of establishing the cost relationships as between what the farmer is selling and what he is buying had really been a little bit more effective up to that time than those that had been followed elsewhere. We think they still are.
If we were called upon to deal with wheat, we would deal with it in exactly the same manner. We have all the records with regard to the prices of wheat back in this three-year period. We would take that as the basis. We have the records, so far as they are available to anyone, of the costs of production of wheat in that period. We would compare the present costs of production with the costs then. I do not say that would prove that the farmer is entitled to some support. It might be possible that it would. Nevertheless, that would be the plan thjt would be followed.

I greatly appreciate that statement. It is becoming more definite all the time. We have more or less been wandering around in the,dark because we did not have anything definite to work on. In effect, the minister has told us that the base period for computing this necessity is that of 1942, 1943 and 1944. Has the minister at any place put on record the figures which obtained with respect to wheat in those years or in that base period?

They are on record in the report. I have the report here for every year since 1914. They are on record, and I presume hon. members have them. They keep quoting them all the time-for example, when it was stated here the other day that the net return to farmers in the last year, 1950, was lower than it was in 1949. If that

quotation is taken from a document, it is taken from the report of the bureau of statistics. In that report of the bureau of statistics all the farm products are dealt with. They can tell you exactly what the price of wheat was at that particular time, averaged over a period. They can also tell you what the costs were over that period of time, in so far as they have figured them. It is those figures that we use as the basis when we start to compute what the position is.

It seems to me that this is an appropriate place for them to be placed on the record. I refer to the figures showing what the farmers received for their wheat and the cost of production.

At that time the Danes would not permit any of the breeding stock to leave Denmark. We got these Swedish hogs, which are of a similar type, and brought them here for the purpose of satisfying some people, one of whom was an hon. member in the house at the time, who thought these hogs were particularly good.
They were brought here, and we carried on the breeding of them until such time as we were satisfied that they were not any improvement on our own Yorks. I recall dealing with the matter in the house, and pointing out that, in connection with the Landrace, the litters were smaller in number, but the pigs were larger when they came. But when we took the two facts into consideration, first that our litters were greater in number, when everything was taken into consideration the outcome of it all was that we thought our own Yorks suited our situation better.
I am told no more of the purebred Land-race are left, but that we have a hybrid which is a cross between the Chester white and the Landrace hog, and that experiments are still being carried on with it. It is not the purebred type we brought here, but a type having some of the characteristics of the Landrace.
I do not know that I can give any particular reason for continuing the experiments. It could happen that at some time we might be producing hogs for a different market, or a market different from that for which we have produced them over the years that have gone by. For that reason perhaps it might be well to continue the experimental work in connection with different types in case that, in certain sections of Canada, we might advise their production. However, I cannot give any better reason than that.

I was out to the farm several weeks ago and saw what appeared to be a cross. They are a lop-eared hog, and look very much like the original Landrace.
Then I would draw to the minister's attention another point, namely, that most of the

Supply-Agriculture
pens in the hog barn are supplied with shavings litter. In my experience with suckling pigs the use of these shavings is dangerous. Many instances have been brought to my attention where little pigs got some of the shavings or sawdust in their intestines or stomachs, and that just about finishes them. I know of many cases where that has happened.
As this is more or less a model farm, and one to which there are many visitors, I suggest there should be straw litter. People go to the experimental farm to see what is done there, and then they return to their homes and follow that example. I feel that if they use these shavings it will lead to trouble.

I am told we have not
had any experiences such as the hon. member has described. There is only one reason of course why they are using shavings. They would prefer to use straw, for a number of reasons, one of the chief ones being that mentioned by the hon. member. It is better to be doing at the experimental farm what the farmer should do at his own farm. We would prefer to have straw for bedding purposes for all the livestock; but I am told it is not possible, or that certainly it is very difficult to get straw for all the purposes for which it is used.
In any advice given to farmers it is always pointed out that straw can be more easily secured, on the ordinary farm, and that it is better to use it in any case because, first of all, it can be used more readily as manure than can the shavings. Advice is given out along those lines. But practical experience has been that they must have some bedding in the form of what is generally known as excelsior or shavings.

I looked at the hogs out there, and I wondered why they were being kept at all. I looked through the different litters and I did not see one of more than four or five. They may have been there, but I did not see them. The litters are uneven, and I thought it was poor production-very poor production. The quality of the hogs was poor. I do not know why they would want to continue to experiment with that kind of hog.

It must be kept in mind that an experimental farm is operated for purposes somewhat different from those of the ordinary farm. Experiments are carried on, for example, in connection with inbreeding, and the results may be very bad. But it is done so that they may advise people to keep away from the very thing they are doing in their experimental work. It is carried on to demonstrate the actual results.

Perhaps that does not apply so much at the central farm as it does in some of the others. For instance, at Saskatoon the college is operated in connection with a sixteen-hundred acre farm. Provision is made there to bring in hogs from different farms throughout the area. They are all fed alike, and we indicate the results of the different types of breeding carried on by individual farmers. We show the results of feeding as applied to hogs bred in certain ways.
All that kind of work is carried on. One can go to the central farm and see pens of hogs he probably would not want to have on his own farm-but that is probably why they are there. They would be there to serve as an example, so that the farmer would know it would not be a good thing to have them.

Experimental farms service-
21. Central experimental farm, operation and! maintenance, $1,686,674.

What experiments are being carried on in connection with the feeding of livestock, including hogs, at the central experimental farm? I believe it is doing an excellent job in developing new strains of grain and seed, but I do feel that in connection with the feeding of hogs, cattle, sheep and poultry not enough experimental work is being done. I feel that the farm should do more experimental work along these lines.

We have certain livestock at the central experimental farm. We have Ayrshire and Holstein dairy cattle, and we also have Shorthorns. In this particular area we pay perhaps more attention to dairy farming, but experimental work is carried on to assist farmers in the matter of breeding. We do not do much artificial insemination as that is done at Kemptville by the provincial government. They have an experiment there which I have looked over on one or two occasions. It is getting good results and is of considerable assistance to the people of the area.
We also have hogs at the farm, as has been indicated by the previous discussion, and we advise with regard to breeding. We do not make a practice of putting out a considerable number of sires. On occasion we import livestock in order to improve the breed in the country generally. We place the sires that we import at different farms across the country, and some are placed here in Ottawa.

I am thinking particularly of feeding and rations experiments

that might be carried on in an effort to find out what best results could be obtained. This is the type of work the farm could carry out most effectively and I wonder if the minister would just comment on what is being done.
That type of experimental work is being carried out at all the experimental farms.
Are any bulletins issued?

Bulletins indicating the
progress reports are issued to all who write in for them.

I notice there are 506
employees at the farm and I was wondering what system they have to prevent people walking over one another.

Five hundred and six may look like a large number, but when you see the buildings there and know the different purposes for which they are used you will understand that it is not. It is the headquarters for our experimental farm work right across the country and the staffs necessary to carry on that work at headquarters are here. A very considerable amount of experimental work is done which requires the employment of persons. One only has to go out there and see the number of people moving about to realize that there have to be quite a number of attendants to take care of the shrubbery, flowers, livestock and everything associated with the farm.

I happened to be there on one occasion last winter, on a rather cold day, and when I went into the horse barn I found quite a few of them asleep in a stall. I do not know whether they were being kepi there as surplus.

It might all depend on
when you were out there. I recall as a boy that it was a custom on all farms, that is those on which I worked in Ontario, to have a nap in the straw in one of the stalls after you had had your lunch. There is irregular feeding to be carried on and some of those men may have been up at unusual hours. They may have done their work before most of us got up and were taking a nap in the middle of the day.
I would recommend that they do not let the public see them because it might create a wrong impression. I was not anxious to see them, but I could not help it.

last year from the central experimental farm?

speakeroldname: Mr. Matthew MacLean (for Mr. Winkler) moved
