speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the order for second reading of this bill was called the last time private bills were being considered, I asked that this one be allowed to stand. I did so because I had made a study of the *case, and I have studied it further since Tuesday evening. In fact, I feel that it is a bill which this house should not pass without further consideration. The evidence which we have received concerning this case is a bulky volume of eighty-six pages. As one who has read every page of it, I can say that it is not recommended reading. Indeed, I shall give the undertaking that I will not quote from this evidence in speaking to the bill now before the house.
I do want to say a few things about the case, and I want to offer a suggestion which I shall put in the form of an amendment to the motion for second reading. These two people were married quite some time ago, and lived together for a number of years, but in due course drifted apart. In the early years of their married life the husband appears to have left the wife on a number of occasions, particularly when she was ill. As a matter of fact, that statement is authenticated in a judgment of one of the courts of the province of Quebec, in connection with a separation granted to these two people in 1947. In his judgment the judge said:
. . . considering, moreover, that the proof establishes the defendant inexcusably neglected his wife during her frequent periods of illness . . .
I suggest that that fact be borne in mind, that a judge of one of the courts of the province of Quebec recognized that this man had inexcusably neglected his wife. I point out also that at one stage of the game this man sought to get an annulment of his marriage. I am not sure whether it was a civil court or a church court to which he applied for the annulment. I may say that the evidence seems to indicate this was a mixed marriage. But at any rate the request of the husband for an annulment of the marriage was declined.
I ask the house to note that, after that bit of background, it is the husband who is applying to the parliament of Canada for a

Private Bills
divorce from his wife. He is charging her with adultery. Indeed, in his petition to the Senate of Canada he names two other men as co-respondents. There are matters of detail in connection with that charge that have a bearing on the case, but I do not wish to go into any great detail because it makes a lurid story, the kind which I do not think should be recited in this House of Commons. Indeed, cases of this kind convince me more than ever that we should not be dealing with these matters at all. They should be before an appropriate court of justice.
There is one other important element in this case, and that is that at the time that the separation was granted by a Quebec court the husband was ordered to pay the wife *the sum of $25 per week for her maintenance and support. The evidence seems to indicate that that order had been carried out, and is still being carried out, by the husband. However, it also seems clear that if this divorce is granted he will no longer be under a legal obligation to pay that money. The woman will no longer be his wife, so he will no longer be liable for her support and maintenance. I understand there is that difference between a court order for money to be paid to a wife and a court order for money to be paid to the children. In the latter case, the order still holds even after a divorce. In this case, I understand that if the husband gets the divorce he is free of the legal obligation to continue to pay the $25 per week to his wife.
It may be said that that is the reason the woman is contesting the case. I want to say that when one reads the evidence, he does not feel that the misconduct is all on one side. In my opinion, there is misconduct on both sides. At any rate, the position of the woman is quite clear, that if this divorce is granted she will be without any guaranteed means of support. The evidence seems to indicate that she is in poor health-indeed, she had been for a number of years prior to the separation which was granted by a Quebec court. As I have already said, the Quebec judge drew particular attention to that fact. I may say that I have had some correspondence about this case. I understand it is the intention of the woman to continue contesting it as long as it is possible to do so. I understand from the correspondence I have had concerning this case that the lawyer for the man made a promise, if I might call it that, to the members of the Senate committee to the effect that after the divorce went through his client would continue to provide for the support and maintenance of the wife. I am told, however, that the lawyer for the woman has tried to get the

man to sign a document to that effect and that he has refused to do so. Maybe there are good reasons why he should make that refusal. Nevertheless, it leaves the woman in the position that, if the divorce is granted, she will have no guarantee that her former husband will be required to support her. He may continue to do so, in keeping with the promise that his lawyer appears to have made to members of the Senate committee. But of course the Senate committee could not hold him to that commitment and he will be under no legal obligation.
In view of all the circumstances, and in view of the fact that the case exercised the Senate committee to the extent of eighty-six pages of printed evidence, I certainly feel that we must give the case fairly close consideration in this house. As to the evidence of adultery itself, I think that anyone who would take the time to read this volume would admit that it is inconclusive and contradictory. I for one cannot say whether or not the alleged adultery took place; and on the basis of the evidence, I would not be prepared to take a position one way or the other. In the light of all that, I feel that further consideration must be given to this case.
It might be pointed out to me that that is what happens when the House of Commons gives second reading to a bill of this kind and subsequently refers it to the standing committee on miscellaneous private bills, namely that that committee does the job of so-called careful consideration. We know that that committee passes in batches bills that are uncontested. It so happens, of course, that this case is likely to be contested before that committee. I understand that the practice of that committee is that, when a case is contested, it is singled out and those who wish to appear are permitted to do so. I believe that the respondent and her lawyer intend to appear before that committee.
Some hon. members might say to me: Well, since that is the practice of the committee, what are you worrying about? Why do you not just let this bill have second reading, let it go to that committee and let them consider it? I wish to answer that argument by reminding hon. members that the practice is almost invariable that a bill that gets second reading from the house is passed by the committee to which it is referred. It goes to the committee with the approval of the principle of the bill, and that fact is brought to the attention of the committee by those who want to see it get through. In other words, the chances of such a bill being defeated in a committee-as will

be seen if one looks at the practices of this committee and the house-are	indeed
extremely slender. I therefore feel that instead of sending this bill to the committee, with the approval that it would have if we gave it second reading, we should1 not now give this bill its second reading but that we should rather send the subject matter of the bill to the committee. If we do that, we will be giving the man, the petitioner, his right to appear before that committee along with his lawyer, and to try to persuade that committee to recommend that the bill be reintroduced.
I suggest that that procedure is fairer to the man himself than it would be if we were simply to vote against second reading and kill the bill. If, without any intermediate opportunity for further inquiry, I had to make the choice between passing or opposing this bill, I would oppose it. Hon. members know that I have said that despite my dislike for the way in which we deal with divorce in this house-it is my feeling that we should not be dealing with it here at all- I have taken the position that in the absence of any clear case against a bill, we should vote for it; and every time there has been a vote on a divorce bill I have voted for it.
But as I say, I have made a careful study of this case; and although I do not see tremendous virtue oh either side, I for one feel that we would not be properly exercising our function as a judicial body if we were to pass this bill as it now stands. But as I said, although I would take that stand, I feel that we must be fair to both sides. We would be doing what the wife wants if we defeated the bill. But the man might say: Well, not many members of the House of Commons studied this case; only two or three of them did so; and no one there stated my side of it. All right. We will give the man his chance to state his side of the case if we send to the committee the subject matter of the bill.
The difference between sending the bill itself and the subject matter, as I have already pointed out, is well known to hon. members. If we send the bill, it already has House of Commons approval and the chances are a thousand to one that the committee will pass it. But if we send not the bill but the subject matter, the committee must start from scratch. The bill itself is dead at that point. It can come back into the house, but only on the basis of the committee's recommending that the bill be reintroduced. That can be done. If the man and his lawyer can persuade the standing committee on miscellaneous
Private Bills
private bills that that should be done, when it comes back to the house I will accept their judgment.
Someone may say: Why do you not accept the judgment of the members of the committee of the other place? I have respect for what they have done. From my study of this case I feel that they have gone into it carefully. I sense a deep concern on their part for the livelihood of this woman. That aspect comes out several times in questions that hon. senators asked. But even so, even though I respect the thorough and judicial job that was done by the committee of the other place, as a member of the House of Commons I feel that I have a right to ask that the committee of this house go into this bill. After all we are, in a sense, a court of two hundred and sixty-two judges being called upon to pass upon this matter. Surely the least we should do is to have our own committee which deals with these matters go into this case thoroughly.
At the risk of repeating myself, Mr. Speaker, I wish to make the point that it is not satisfactory to me to give this bill second reading and to send it to the committee. That procedure makes its approval by the committee almost a foregone conclusion. Under that circumstance the woman and her lawyer could appear before that committee, but their chances of getting the committee to upset the bill would be extremely slim. If, however, we send to the committee the subject matter of the bill rather than the bill itself, the man and his lawyer can appear, as well as the woman and her lawyer, and they are on a more equal footing. The man has the chance, if he can prove to that committee that he has a case, to persuade them to recommend the reintroduction of the bill. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that we must look at this thing in a judicial capacity as best we can. We must assess the evidence that is given to us and try to decide who is right and who is wrong. That is extremely difficult to do on the basis of contradictory and inconclusive evidence.
One feels doubt about several of the witnesses that appeared, as to their credibility, but despite that, I look at these two parties, neither of whom I know or have ever met, and I say to myself: If we approve the divorce, that is the end of the marriage, and that may be the end of $25 a week that the woman gets to live on. She is in her fifties; she is in poor health. Therefore if we take that course we may be making a mistake that we cannot repair. Do we do a wrong to the man if we deny the divorce, or if we require him to appear before a

Private Bills
committee of this house to prove his case? I think not. He has a separation now. He is not being forced to live with this woman whom he no longer loves. The most that we do by way of penalizing him is to prevent him from having the opportunity to remarry. There is no indication in the evidence, at any rate, that that is the purpose of this petition.
Someone might say: we do him the wrong of forcing him to continue to pay that $25 a week. He has said to the Senate committee that he is prepared to support his wife. If he feels he should not be so obligated all he has to do is to apply again to the courts of Quebec for a reconsideration of the court order that was made in 1947. So, all things considered, I think the fair, most objective, most judicial thing that this house can do is to deny this bill its second reading at this time-I emphasize the words "at this time"-and instead to refer its subject matter to our committee so that it can be discussed there.
There are few cases that I have read this session, and I have read a good many of them., that are as replete as this one is with the sort of evidence that one does not want to quote; so I have kept strictly away from that and I have tried to discuss this case in as dignified a way as I could in view of its nature. I have tried to be fair with it in my own mind and in my presentation of it, and I say to the house quite sincerely that I think my suggestion is the one that the house should follow.
If I were asking the house to vote against this bill and kill it, someone might say: You are unfair to the man. All right; I am asking the house to ask our committee to give it further consideration, but to give it consideration in such a manner that the man and woman will both appear before that committee on an equal footing, and have a chance to start from scratch before a committee of this house. Therefore, Mr. Speaker,-
May I ask the hon. gentleman one or two questions?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Certainly.

The first question is:	Does
he feel that there is not that abundance of evidence in favour of the petitioner that is required in order to over-balance her evidence; that is, if the hon. gentleman were trying this case himself would he feel convinced that the petitioner had proved his case? The next question is this-he made some suggestion as to both parties being guilty:	Is there evidence indicating that the
husband himself in this case was guilty of

adultery? The third question is:	Is there
evidence there which would indicate that there was connivance by the husband in this case? The reason I am asking these questions is that I know the hon. gentleman has given the matter serious consideration. In any matter to which he does give consideration he has a full and perfect grasp of the situation. If these questions were to be answered by the hon. gentleman in the affirmative then I would think that his proper motion would be to give this bill the six months hoist.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I thank the hon. member
for Inverness-Richmond for the honour he has done me in putting these questions to me. In answer to his first question I may say that I am not satisfied there is abundance of evidence in favour of the petitioner. If the hon. member had asked me the opposite question, is there abundance of evidence in favour of the wife's innocence of misconduct I would have to give the same answer. Mr. Speaker, Bill No. 321 is to incorporate Champion Pipe Line Corporation Limited, under the general terms of the pipe lines legislation enacted by the house.
The object of the bill is to construct a pipe line to carry gas from the Alberta fields to Vancouver, British Columbia. The incorporators are set out in the bill, and they will be the first directors. I should point out that they are all prominent Canadians, and are well known probably to most of us.
The powers are set out in particular in section 6 of the bill, and with permission of the house I should like to read only lines 32, 33 and 34, which state:
-provided that the main pipe line or lines for the transmission and transportation of gas and oil shall be located entirely within Canada.
I am sure the proposed route will be of interest to hon. members from the west. It runs from Edmonton to Calgary, Pincher Creek, Crowsnest, Michel, Natal, McGilli-vray, Fernie, Cranbrook, with a spur to Kimberley, Creston, Sirdar, Kootenay lake, Salmo, Ymir, Cascade, Grand Forks, Simil-kameen, Cawston, Princeton and Hope, where the line will join the Fraser valley and proceed by the Fraser valley to Vancouver.
The safeguards surrounding this legislation are, of course, well known to the house; so that at this late stage I do not think I need go into them. Suffice it to say that if this bill is referred to the committee which will examine it in detail, we will have our experts there, the engineers and others, and be in a position to give the committee full details on any questions that may be raised. In seeking this incorporation we are merely acting under the legislation provided by this parliament; and if it is your pleasure we hope eventually to have the right to compete with the other companies which have obtained similar bills, under similar provisions and conditions.

I should like to say a very few words in support of this bill. I do so because the applicants for this charter propose to follow what we may call a Canada-first route from the province of Alberta to Vancouver on the Pacific coast.
I believe those of us who opposed applications for other charters where the route was to go at least in part through the United States will support an application such as that now before us.


As the sponsor has pointed out, several groups have now obtained charters who propose to build a pipe line to the west coast by an all-Canadian route, so the fear expressed during the debates last year that there might be a monopoly no longer exists. There are now several companies from which to choose, and most of them propose to build through Canada. It is agreed, I think, that at least in the near future there will be only one oil line and one gas line to the west coast.
I would point out to you, Mr. Speaker, and to the house, that there has been a great change this year in the attitude adopted toward these applications for a pipe line charter. The standing committee of this house on railways, canals and telegraph lines has written into three charters amendments similar to the wording read by the sponsor a few moments ago, providing that the main pipe line must be located entirely within Canada. Then one group applying for incorporation under the name Independent Pipe Line Company actually brought their bill to the other place with those words written in. Tonight we are considering a charter which was similarly amended in the other place. For the first time the Senate has written into one of these bills words which provide that the main pipe line must be located entirely within Canada. As a matter of fact there is only one pipe line bill before the house at the present time which does not meet that requirement. The bill to which I refer is-
Perhaps the hon. member might leave that until a later time.

Well, I think I am entitled to mention that the name of the company concerned is the Border Pipeline Corporation. This change in attitude is very significant, and I believe it is in line with the beliefs and interests of the Canadian people.
Pipe line bills passed in earlier sessions did not contain this Canada-first provision, though in some cases the sponsors pledged themselves to follow an all-Canadian route. There were sponsors of other bills, of course, who did not do so, notably the Alberta Natural Gas Company and Prairie Trans-misision Lines Limited.
I trust that when the board of transport commissioners come to deal with an application for the right to lay a pipe line they will take notice of this changed attitude which certainly exists in this house and I believe also in the other place, and will grant a permit only for a Canada-first route.

Certainly there is no excuse for the board of transport commissioners to follow any other course.
The same is true of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), to whom a company must apply for permission to export oil or gas to the United States. I hope he too will take note of the changed attitude this year and will refuse to grant any company permission to export oil or gas from Canada unless the main pipe line of that company is laid in Canadian soil.

The next greatest amount that has to be accounted for is the fluid milk. Between the two of them they take up the greater part of the milk production. After that we put the surplus which is left over into cheese, ice cream and canned milk of one kind and another, and into powdered milk. So far as all these commodities are concerned1, we have sufficient for our own needs, and fortunately for us at the present time we are able to consume the greater part of them in this country.
When it comes to meat products, which were mentioned as well, we eat all the pork that we produce at present. We do not eat anything like all the beef that we produce. A very considerable part of our beef goes to the United States, but the other products are being largely consumed in this country, and the price which is being obtained for them does not suggest to our people that they could gain very much by producing say 5 per cent or 10 per cent more and shipping it out. There is not much inclination on the part of our producers to want to get into that position. They are producing what can be marketed in


this country and what can be marketed in the United States at a better price in some cases than can be obtained here, and I do not know of any way in which you could encourage them to do differently. I do not know that we want to encourage them to do differently from what they are doing.

Would the minister consider it appropriate to discuss the question of fertilizers on this item? It looks to me as though fertilization would enter into it. Particularly I should like to know whether or not Canada is producing enough nitrates to enable our farmers to maintain the fertility of their soil against the depletion that normally takes place through raising the large crops that we are raising. If we are not producing enough nitrates, then obviously we are running down our soil. Has the minister any information on the point?

We have scarcely enough of potash and phosphates. We could make use of more. We have a surplus of nitrogen. We are producing all the nitrogen necessary for the production of fertilizers. As regards other ingredients, apart from phosphates and potash, we have no difficulty in obtaining a supply sufficient to take care of our needs.

Has the minister's department any information as to the general use of these fertilizers? For instance, are the people in Alberta restoring to the soil, in a general way, enough nutrients to prevent a wasting away of the fertility of the soil? Has the minister collected that information, or is that turned over to the provinces?

We have here the tonnage of distribution, but I do not know that that answers the question asked. We carry on experimental work at all our experimental farms in connection with the effect of the use of fertilizers. Last year for example I travelled all the way from Ottawa to Fairbanks, Alaska, by motorcar, and I stopped off at most of the illustration stations throughout Alberta, up to British Columbia and right on up into the Yukon. I found that at every one of those illustration stations they were carrying on experiments in connection with the utilization of fertilizers.
One thing they told me at every place I stopped was that their experiments indicated that the best fertilizer is barnyard manure, and that all these other things that are talked about, and for which people are paying big prices, were not as useful as barnyard manure-or, at least, if you did not have barnyard manure, other things did not produce as good results.
Other fertilizers are well advertised by the people who sell them. I think there may

be some reason why we do not make as much use of barnyard manure as we did at one time. But that is what our experimental farms and illustration stations are doing-they are determining these things. When I have driven along the highways in Ontario and in the maritime provinces I have seen plots on which cages have been placed in order to check carefully the growth of grasses, as a result of the utilization of different kinds of fertilizers.
That practice is carried on continuously and, while some of this work may be done by the provinces, it is a work we are doing through our experimental farm service right across the country.

I have raised the question for the reason the minister has given. Everyone knows that in the last fifty years we have stopped using horses. As a result, the fertility which is restored to the farm through having horses is lost. Then, we are apparently going out of the production of cattle-that is, if we increase the use of margarine in place of butter.
So far as I can see, all these matters militate against the maintenance of fertility of the land. I cannot think of any other item under which this matter might more properly be discussed. I am alarmed lest we are running our soil down at a far more rapid rate than we can afford. That is why I am asking the minister if some other discoveries have been made in connection with fertilizers, as a result of which we could maintain the fertility of our land, notwithstanding that we are producing fewer livestock as the years go by.

I think the answer to the point the hon. member has in mind is to be found in a statement I have here, which points out that the use of fertilizer in Canada has more than doubled since 1940, having increased from 300,000 tons in that year to 765,000 tons in 1950. It is estimated, according to this statement, that the demand for fertilizer in 1951 may be still higher than it was in 1950. That figure is two and a half times higher than it was ten years ago.

I had the matter impressed on my mind particularly in connection with the production of beets in the Lethbridge area. Farms that a few years ago produced 23 or 24 tons to the acre, for some reason or other have fallen away in their potential production. The people find it difficult to know why this is happening, because they are putting a good deal of artificial fertilizer
Supply-Agriculture
on the soil to raise their beets. There must be some definite depreciation in the quality of the soil taking place.
If this is so, then it seems to me a matter of major importance, and all the departments of agriculture across the nation should give the closest attention to it.
I should like to know whether, with all this additional use of fertilizer, we are maintaining the fertility of our soil. I do not suppose the minister has information from which he could answer my question. It is a matter that should be looked into by his department.
Are we adopting measures which will keep fertilizer costs down to the point at which encouragement will be given the average farmer to use it extensively? I am referring particularly to nitrates, potash and phosphates.

The claim is made in
Ontario-and we think with some truth- that they are maintaining the fertility of the soil in a major part of that province. That, of course, is a general statement. There may be areas in which it is not being done, and there may be other areas in which it is being built up to the point where it is pretty good soil. I think the same would be true across Canada. I happen to farm in an area where most people think fertilizer is not required at all. Some others are making use of fertilizer. However, most people argue that there is not enough difference in what they produce as a result of using fertilizer to pay them for doing so. The result is that they do not use it. That is in a part of the prairie section where the fertility of the soil is high, and where in some areas that soil is very deep. Even if two or three inches were to blow off the top, it would not do much more than improve the farm. The fertility of the soil is the same in some areas, even if one went down one hundred feet. In those districts one does not talk a great deal about fertilizers.
But we know that where there is erosion, and where there is a top soil of only three or four inches, if that top soil is carried away in any way, whether it be by wind, water or some other means, there is a reduction in the productivity, and ways must be found of putting something back.
On the other hand, if you grow the same crop over and over again without putting anything back, the land will cease to produce that kind of crop to advantage. There are all kinds of ways in which productivity can be kept up; but in most areas the productivity of the soil is maintained at about what it has been on the average over the years.

The fact that more and more
tractors are being used on the farms today, and also that we are raising fewer horses and cattle, accounts for the lack of barnyard manure. Since it is not manufactured, naturally it cannot be put on the land, and for that reason some other method must be adopted to maintain the soil. I know that in my own district we have used quite a lot of fertilizer during the last ten or twelve years. Last fall we had what I consider a very important meeting at the agricultural school at Vermilion, attended by the councils of three large municipal districts as well as the service boards of those districts and many dttiers interested in agriculture. We also had the superintendent of the Lethbridge experimental station and the publisher of the Lethbridge Herald, who took a leading part in that meeting. That evening quite a dinner was put on, attended by a couple of hundred farmers, townspeople and others vitally interested in agriculture. Those two gentlemen from Lethbridge gave a very interesting description of soil conservation in their district. I believe that is being followed up this month with another meeting, and many people are hoping something worth while will be done in connection with soil conservation. If we can develop something in our district, of course, it will be circulated to other districts in that area. I feel that the fertility of the soil must be maintained, and that many people who today are mining the soil must get busy and learn to conserve instead. If they do not, I am afraid the future of agriculture will not be very bright. We have to do everything possible to conserve the soil and improve marketing conditions so agriculture may retain its rightful place in our economy.

Perhaps I had better read what has been placed before me. I was waited upon by the president of the Cumberland county farmers association, Mr. Rae McCunn, the vice-president, Mr. Walton Allan, and the secretary-treasurer, Mr. Carl Embree. After they had had a meeting with the agriculturists in that county, this is what they had to say with respect to fertilizer:
Fertilizer prices are advancing and we believe that one of the main causes of this increase is due to the increase in the price of nitrate of ammonia. After the last war the government sold plants manufacturing this product to private business firms and the prices immediately jumped from $74 to $91 per ton. Through pressure brought about by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture prices dropped back to $74.50 per ton. During the past two or three years prices have steadily climbed until at present this product is costing $92 per ton.

As I understand the statement that was read, it is to the effect that nitrates were made at low cost during the war, that they were made in plants that were then owned and controlled by the government, that those plants were later disposed of and that the costs have been higher.
The prices were reduced after the plants were taken over by private interests, and they have since been increased to almost $100 a ton.

All I can say about the matter at the moment is that it is true that at

one time the plants were owned, operated and controlled by the government. 30.	Grants to fairs and exhibitions, under such 'terms and conditions as may be approved by the governor in council and subject to allocation by the treasury board, $614,400.
How many class A fairs and how many class B fairs has the minister? Have any been added to the group?

There is one class A fair in Prince Edward Island at Charlottetown. Is it just the numbers in each province that are desired or the places of them? Class of fair: A's, Prince Edward Island, one; Quebec, four; Ontario, seven; Manitoba, one; Saskatchewan, two; Alberta, two; British Columbia, one; making a total of eighteen. Class B fairs: Nova Scotia, four; Quebec, twelve; Ontario, twenty-one; Manitoba, three; Saskatchewan, eight; Alberta, five; British Columbia, two; total fifty-five.
Are there* any class A or class B fairs in New Brunswick?

We pay on a somewhat different basis in New Brunswick. The New Brunswick people did not desire to go on operating on the same basis as we operate in the other provinces. There were special situations existing there.
Is it commensurate?

I think so. It works out at just about the same as they would get if they classified their fairs 'as "A" and "B." But they have a different classification, and we have accepted it as being similar to what is being followed in other provinces. The show mentioned here is the New Brunswick cattle show at Frederiction.

I am pleased that the cattle show at Fredericton has a grant of $10,000. I believe it was increased a year or two ago. It seems to me the subsidy being paid the maritime winter fair at Amherst is entirely inadequate, having regard to present-day costs. The amount is only $5,500. It is probably by far the most important agricultural fair in all the maritime provinces, and the oldest fair of

its kind in Canada. It has done more than any other organization to improve the quality of livestock.
Some of the directors have spoken to me with regard to their costs, and the difficulties they are having in operating this fair which serves Nova Scotia and New Brunswick and in an even greater measure serves Prince Edward Island. Each of those provinces draws prizes in almost equal amounts from the maritime winter fair. It seems to me it should be given a much larger grant than is provided in the estimates. People who are interested in agriculture attend this show in large numbers. They come from the three maritime provinces, and they look forward to the minister's making a special visit. However, in recent years they have been disappointed when he has not been able to be present. I presume he has other functions to perform that he considers are more important than his presence at the maritime winter fair. Could not arrangements be made to give a larger grant to that fair than is provided in the estimates?

I notice that the provincial cattle show at Fredericton is in receipt of a grant of $10,000. I have no complaint against that; they deserve it. But there is no special grant for Prince Edward Island, because it is in with the other maritime provinces, and is included with the maritime winter fair at Amherst. As the hon. member for Cumberland has said, that winter fair has done a great deal to improve the livestock of this country. From time to time this matter has been discussed by breeders. They have appealed to the hon. member for Cumberland and to me to see if they could get something additional for the maritime winter fair. I hope the minister will give consideration to this suggestion in his supplementary estimates.

I should like to express my appreciation of the maritime winter fair at Amherst. I know our people in New Brunswick look forward to it every year, and it is known as one of the big events in the agricultural world.
The hon. member for Queens seemed to question the $10,000 granted to the provincial cattle show at Fredericton. As I understood from the minister a moment ago, New Brunswick is in a position different from the other provinces. The only grant we receive is this $10,000, whereas the other provinces are receiving grants for "A" and "B" fairs and provincial summer fairs. I think it will be seen that Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick have received grants for fairs in addition to those at

Amherst and Charlottetown, or wherever they may be. On the other hand we receive a grant only for the one at Fredericton in compensation for not being allowed grants for other fairs.

That is right. We were
paying on one "A" fair and three "B" fairs to a total amount of $11,000 in New Brunswick. We made an arrangement with them whereby we would pay $10,000 on one fair.
We lost money.

We saved a thousand
dollars on the transaction. But it suited them better in New Brunswick than any other arrangement, and we agreed to the suggestion. We saved around $1,000 in doing it.
And, to complete the picture, would you tell us what they received, in the aggregate?

I gave the figures a moment ago. For Bridgewater fair in Nova Scotia the amount is $2,500; Oxford fair, $2,187.75; Sydney, $901.12; Truro, $2,500; Amherst winter fair, $5,500. If they are added up it is about $3,000 more.

Why is Oxford fair, which is considered the best county fair in the maritime provinces, if not in the whole of Canada, receiving only $2,187.75, while these other fairs which are not as large or not as important receive $2,500? This would not appear to me to be a large grant for Oxford fair.
It is on the basis of improvements. We pay 50 per cent of improvements.
Does that mean improvements to quarters?

Improvements and repairs
to buildings, including the putting up of new buildings and the repairing of buildings already in existence.
Which fair in New Brunswick had the department been previously subsidizing, or paying a grant to, as a 1-A fair?
Saint John.

As the minister probably
realizes, Saint John fair was interrupted by the second world war. Plans are under way to have it resume some time in the future. I am wondering if the present allocation to the provincial exhibition at Fredericton will in any way prejudice the chances of the Saint John fair receiving a further grant in future as a class 1-A fair.

The arrangement at present is that we accept the approval of the province.

I presume that if the province withdraws its approval we might talk about something else.

33. Agricultural economics, $510,433.

I have in my hand a copy of the Country Guide for May, 1951, in which
I find this statement:
The U.S. Department of Agriculture discloses that the cost of bringing a pound of beef from the farm to the retail counter is now nearly four times as high as it was in 1945, the margin having increased-from 6 to 22-5 cents per pound in five years . . .
Secretary Brannan released some figures which may help city people to understand what is happening to price relationships. Milk doubles in price within a few hours after it leaves the farm. For the com inside a 19-cent can the farmer gets 21 cents. His share of a can of 16-cent tomatoes is:
3 cents. Onions which cost the consumer 6 cents a pound left the farm at a cent a pound. The same thing applies to clothing. The cotton in a shirt costing from $3.50 to $4 brought the farmer 30' cents. The wheat in a 15-eent loaf has enriched the man who produced it by 2| cents.
Armed with this information American farm leaders are making some very caustic comments. Statistical analyses of this nature are not available in Canada . . .
That is the point I want to bring to the minister's attention.
. . . but The Guide would recommend it as a good exercise for the large numbers of technical people, capable of doing this kind of work, now on the payroll at Ottawa.
I imagine that type of work would be done under this vote, and I am wondering how much has been done or is being done at present.
As I understand what has been stated by the hon. member, it is to the effect that in the United States they have worked out certain relationships between costs and prices.

The spread between what the producer gets and what the consumer pays, and th.e relationship of that spread as it changes from year to year. This indicates that in the United States is has increased, and apparently we have no comparable statistics in Canada.

Well, I do not know that we have no statistics. Any statistics we have would be prepared by the bureau of statistics. We utilize their statistics in our prices support board in working out relationships between costs and prices. The price of milk is referred to in detail in the article just read. The control of milk prices is with the' provinces and always has been, with the exception of a short period during the war.. While the war was on we did take control of milk prices, but that was the first product to be decontrolled and turned back to the

Supply-Agriculture
provinces at the end of the war. The reason for that was that the provinces had boards to handle it.

That is not the point of the question at all. The point is, does the department keep any records or try to obtain any ^records as to the spread between what the producer gets for his product and what the *consumer pays for it from year to year, so the department would know the trend, -whether or not there is a greater spread from ?year to year? That is the kind of economics *on which the department would be well ^advised to have some information, and I think such information would be valuable.

There are some eight or nine products on which we are carrying out investigations, but I repeat that the facts on which we base our investigations are obtained from the bureau of statistics. Those facts are utilized in surveys being made by our economics branch. We have figures in that connection.

Apparently in the United States they consider these figures important. For a number of years now they have kept track of the relationship between what the producer receives and what the consumer pays. That has always been a matter of controversy in this country, and I am sure such information would be valuable.

A report on the nine commodities I mentioned has been published and distributed, along the line of what has been suggested. Some people may think it is not as well done as in the United States; some may think it is better done. I am not prepared to say one way or the other. During the war period we did make very careful studies of those questions in connection with price controls. It may be that in the United States their studies are a little more careful at the present time because they have price controls there, and these things are important in that connection.

I think this information is important not only when you are enforcing price control, but to indicate to the people who is getting the gravy, to use the language *of this article, through the increased prices which consumers are having to pay for many farm products. I am sure farm organizations would find such information very useful in arguing the case for the farmer. Certainly 1 would compliment the department on having made a start last year on this type of work, and I think it should be extended to more products than are under investigation at the present time.

I notice in the details at page 100 that 38 economists are employed under this heading, and I am wondering what functions they perform. I am wondering that because in Newfoundland we have a marketing problem that probably does not exist in any other part of Canada. On the west coast we have three of the principal fertile agricultural areas, with one on the east coast. On the west coast we have the Codroy valley, Stephenville and the Humber area; and when the minister visits Newfoundland I hope he will find it convenient to visit those districts. There he will see land equal to any in Ontario or Quebec, where the possibility of increasing production is very great.
I know from experience that the producers are handicapped by the lack of storage facilities, and also by the lack of refrigerator cars to bring their potatoes to St. John's during the winter season. At present when the potatoes are brought during the winter they are frozen in transit, and of course deteriorate in value. Then on the east coast near St. John's we have another area where agriculture is practised intensively. It is an extraordinary thing, however, that produce from the St. John's area will be sent to Grand Falls, Comer Brook or the lumber camps, while produce from the west coast will be brought all the way to St. John's. I believe the economists could usefully investigate the conditions under which agriculture is being practised in Newfoundland. I have spoken on this subject each time the estimates have been before the committee, and on other occasions when I have had the opportunity.
I want to say that agriculture has been neglected in Newfoundland and is still being neglected. It is capable of improving the conditions of Newfoundlanders more than anything else. The minister, the government and members of this house are familiar with the difficulties under which the fishing industry has been Labouring for these past two years. In fact the fishing industry has been, labouring for a good many years, but agriculture is capable of redressing some of the balance and giving a better balanced economy to Newfoundland.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
We are not dealing with
fishing.

I am dealing with the question of agricultural economics. That is the heading here, and if what I am saying is not agricultural economics I should like to know what it is.
I am only making a comparison. I noticed the parliamentary assistant smiling when I referred to fishing, but after all when we are

talking about economics we can afford to make some comparisons. Agriculture was, as I pointed out before, practised to a greater extent thirty or forty years ago than it is today. There were more farms around the city of St. John's, which has a population of 60,000 and is therefore a big market, forty years ago than there are today. We are bringing into Newfoundland from the other provinces far greater quantities of agricultural produce than are necessary.
The provincial government is not in a position to embark upon a policy because it has not got the direction. It has not got the men, the economists, the trained agriculturists. I hope the minister will see that during his visit, and I trust he will come back with the idea of helping Newfoundland. I do not believe there is a minister in the government who can give more assistance to the improvement of the economy of Newfoundland than the Minister of Agriculture. I have urged him now for two years to visit Newfoundland, and I can say there is no member in this house more pleased than I am to know that he is going there. If he will apply his perspicacity and experience to a study of the conditions in Newfoundland I believe it will be for the benefit of Newfoundlanders generally.

We had three or four
economists in Newfoundland, as no doubt my friend knows, during the greater part of last summer, and we are still carrying on investigations there. We did delay some of the work in connection with production until the census is completed this year because much of the information required on which to base studies will be obtained through the census. The economists have been down there carrying on investigations with regard to the food supplies of the island, the sources from which they come and the extent to which they can be produced on the island. All of that has a bearing of course upon agriculture in the province. While I am down there for three or four days at the beginning of next week I shall look into the matter as far as it is possible to do so in that limited period of time. I am quite sure that I shall benefit from the journey there, and I hope the island will benefit by it as well.

I do not know whether or
not the question I am going to ask has been brought up before. I am sorry to say that I was not here today, but I was at Chalk River looking over that institution and as a result was not able to be here this afternoon. However, I want to bring up a matter under this item. Looking at the details on page
Supply-Agriculture
100, there is an item for printing of departmental reports and other publications. Referring to the summary of standard objects of expenditure and special categories, which was furnished with the estimates, I see that under this item the Department of Agriculture has an expenditure for this year of $485,175, which is the largest amount by a considerable extent for any department with the exception of national defence.
I know of course that the Department of Agriculture publishes a considerable number of pamphlets of various sorts, and of those that have come into my hands the majority are useful publications. I should like the minister to tell the committee what the item of $485,175 covers, and without going into too much detail what publications are involved, in addition of course to the general report of the Department of Agriculture.

I do not know whether I misunderstand the statement that has been made. I understood that the hon. member for Calgary East was discussing the item of printing of departmental reports and other publications on page 100. That item amounts to $21,550. What is the explanation of the $485,000? I did not get the connection.

This same item, printing of departmental reports and other publications, occurs under a very large number of other items in the Department of Agriculture. The total shown in this summary to which I have referred is $485,175.

Of course there are items similar to this one, and they have been covered in all of the votes that we have passed. I assume the total will be somewhere in the neighbourhood of the figure that has been mentioned. I have no reason for saying that is not the correct figure. It will be a considerable amount, and that is natural, as the hon. member has already suggested, in the Department of Agriculture. We have between 700,000 and 800,000 farmers in Canada, and it is our duty to distribute the knowledge we obtain through our experimental farms and otherwise which is going to be helpful to as many of those farmers as are interested. Therefore our printing bill will be considerably higher than that of most other departments. The hon. member has said it is higher than any other department except national defence. That is probably correct, and these are very good reasons why it is correct. There is the matter of distribution to farmers throughout a country as large as ours, and the fact that they are all intimately concerned with what is going on at our experimental farms and elsewhere

Supply-Agriculture
makes it necessary for our publications to be in very considerable number and to be put out in considerable quantity.

If this information has already been put on the record I do not want it to be put on, again, but if it has not I should like to have the minister bring forward, so that it can be put on Hansard as an appendix, the details of the amount of $485,175.

I do not think we should carry the item. I should like to ask some questions after the information has been put on Hansard.
